newsitem.title: FRANCE: French minister accuses Uganda in Zaire crisis.
newsitem.headline: French minister accuses Uganda in Zaire crisis.

text.p: French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette accused Uganda on Thursday of intervening directly to support Zairean rebels seeking to overthrow President Mobutu Sese Seko, a Paris ally.

But de Charette indicated that France, which has been pressing for United Nations intervention to stop hostilities in a move which could save Mobutu's crumbling authority, would not intervene alone in Zaire.

"We demand the respect of Zaire's territorial integrity. What must stop are the interventions of its neighbours, particularly Uganda whose activity on Zairean soil is an established fact," de Charette told the newspaper Ouest-France.

Zaire accused Uganda, as well as Rwanda and Burundi, of sending troops to back Tutsi rebels who have captured a swathe of eastern Zaire and are scoring increasing victories against Mobutu's ill-disciplined army.
Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni denied during a visit to Paris last month that there were any Ugandan troops in Zaire.

Paris believes the key to halting the conflict may lie with Washington which has close ties with Uganda and Rwanda. French analysts said the government believed the United States was trying to edge it out of the last region where France still wielded influence left over from its colonial past.
United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan, encouraged by France, said last Friday in Paris he hoped to persuade U.N. member states to revive a plan to send a multinational force.
But the United States said on Wednesday it was not ready to take part in the force whose official goal was to aid refugees caught up in the fighting in eastern Zaire.
"I see no one is ready to commit itself except France," de Charette told Ouest-France.
"But, because of the context on the ground, a French intervention alone would have more negative effects than positive ones," he said.

The initial plan to send a multinational force collapsed last year when many of an estimated 1.2 million refugees from neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi returned home of their own accord. But more than 200,000 refugees remain trapped in Zaire.
